\section{The night of 2026-10-05: speed, the Delta round, and the fast round v22\secstatus{todo}}
\label{sec:night}
\input{tables/v22_numbers}

\pfstep{Correction: v21 on Delta cannot reach its window as launched} \Cref{sec:status}
projected 22 to 24 hours per pack from the training progress bar, 49 to 59 s. The logged
epoch time is 177 s on every run: the reference arm was at epoch 69 after 3.3 hours of
training. At that pace 1{,}200 epochs take 59 hours against the 48 hour limit, and a pack
stops near epoch 945, short of the registered window of epochs 1{,}000 to 1{,}200. The cause
was read from forty stack dumps of one run over six minutes: in all forty the main thread
sat in the eval-mode train pass, spawning a data-loader worker. That pass rebuilt its loader
every tenth epoch, and on Delta a spawned worker re-imports the software stack from Lustre,
more than twelve minutes each time. It follows from launching the round with one loader
worker; with zero the pass would have been slow but would not have respawned anything. The
epoch times are \texttt{perf/epoch\_seconds} of W\&B project
\texttt{torchcell\_019\_expr\_v21}; the dumps were taken on Delta job 22690625.
\src{notes/experiments.019-simb-multimodal.scripts.v22_readout.md}

\pfstep{Where an epoch went} A profile of the reference run on the GilaHyper cards, then
stack samples of live runs, located five costs, none of them the model's own arithmetic
(\cref{tab:night-timing}). Producing a sample cost 50 ms (a database read, a JSON parse, the
reconstruction of an experiment record with thousands of phenotype values) and was repeated
for every sample every epoch. Decoding each strain's target row from the batch ran as a
Python loop over the strains with about ten points per strain where the CPU waits on the
GPU, 59 to 65 percent of a training process's time once several processes shared a card.
The perturbation operator ran one strain at a time. The epoch metrics ranked a 1{,}100 by
6{,}127 matrix on the CPU three times an epoch. And all six encoder layers built a full
gene-by-gene attention matrix that only the one graph-regularized layer reads. Each was
replaced by a form that computes the same thing, held equal to the original by a test: the
operator and the decode on batched tensors, the ranks on the GPU, the fused attention kernel
on the unregularized layers, and the splits held in memory after one pass. After the changes
the stack samples show the process waiting on the GPU, on the operator's feed-forward block
over every gene of every strain; what is left is the architecture's own work.
\src{notes/experiments.019-simb-multimodal.scripts.gh_profile_cgt_expr.md}

A batch-128 run holds 12.2 GB of card memory against 8.5 GB at batch 32, so three fit on a
card and a fourth runs out of memory. Processes sharing a card take turns on it, so a card
of mixed arms runs every arm at the pace of the slowest; each card below holds one arm.

\pfstep{The state of v21 on Delta} The queue's start estimate for a resubmission was a day
out, so one pack was replaced inside its own running job at 03:58: the four reference runs
of split seeds 0 to 3 were stopped at epoch 70 and restarted from scratch on the new code
with zero loader workers and the splits in memory. They log 38 to 41 s per epoch, 100 s on
every tenth, about 45 s on average, which is 15 hours for 1{,}200 epochs. The other 26
packs were left as launched. Replacing them the same way is prepared and was run without
effect as a check; it needs the author's decision, as does the alternative of canceling and
resubmitting through the queue. The four restarted runs are W\&B \texttt{iuqwl2p8},
\texttt{tdnhpkid}, \texttt{fcq0xkke} and \texttt{0jajrluv}.
\src{experiments/019-simb-multimodal/scripts/delta_v21_inplace_swap.sh}

\pfstep{The rising validation loss on expression is a scale problem} Earlier sections
record that the validation loss bottoms out early and rises while the per-feature Pearson
keeps climbing, and that at its Pearson peak no run beats the per-gene mean on squared
error. A predictor with correlation $r$ to its target minimizes squared error when the ratio
of its spread to the target's equals $r$. On the six saved validation prediction sets, one
scalar was fit on half the validation strains (with a per-gene intercept) and scored on the
other half (\cref{tab:night-shrink}). The expression predictions are 1.4 to 2.2 times too
spread for their correlation; shrinking them by the fitted scalar brings all three
checkpoints below the per-gene mean, to what the correlation allows (for split seed 0,
$1.036 \times (1 - 0.225^2) = 0.983$ against a measured $0.984$). The proteome head has the
opposite sign at its best-validation checkpoint and is under-dispersed. So the ordering the
metric reads is intact and the magnitudes are overfit; calibration can be repaired after
training without changing the Pearson. The same arithmetic states how little is explained:
$r^2$ is 2 to 5 percent of per-gene variance across held-out strains.

\pfstep{Round v22: what a faster batch costs} Every arm is the v21 reference with one
change, on the new code, 1{,}200 epochs unless stated, scored as v21 by the mean validation
Pearson per feature over epochs 1{,}000 to 1{,}200 (\cref{tab:night-arms,tab:night-runs}).
Two to three split seeds per arm size an effect and do not decide one.

\pfstep{Batch 128 needs its learning rate left alone or warmed up} At four times the
reference rate no run launched (3 of 3 split seeds): the prediction spread stayed at zero
from the first epoch. At twice the rate without warmup two of three runs launched and then
returned to the per-gene-mean predictor, at epochs 212 and 658. At the unscaled rate, and
at twice the rate behind a 50-epoch linear warmup, all six runs completed; their window
scores are \nightLrOneWindows{} and \nightWarmupWindows{} on split seeds 0, 1 and 2. The
batch-32 reference on the same code reads \nightRefWindows. Against it the unscaled arm is
\nightLrOneVsRef, and the warmup arm is \nightWarmupVsRef. Three split seeds resolve only
a difference whose sign all three share, which \cref{tab:night-arms} marks with an arrow;
the partition moves the score more than either arm does. What the batch buys is time: 11.4 s
per epoch against 24, three runs to a card in both cases.
\src{experiments/019-simb-multimodal/results/v22_readout.json}

\pfstep{A collapse is a return to the per-gene mean, and the validation loss rewards it}
In the collapsed runs the gradient norm stays between 0.01 and 0.05 and the clip at 10
never engages, so nothing diverges; the prediction spread falls to zero within about 30
epochs and the validation loss returns to 0.2506, the loss of the per-gene-mean predictor.
The runs that keep training sit at a validation loss of 0.254 to 0.257, above it. On
held-out strains the loss prefers the collapsed predictor to the trained one, which is the
scale problem of \cref{tab:night-shrink} seen from the other side. The collapsed runs are
\texttt{l885wzyv}, \texttt{zz9sbrr3}, \texttt{pbqtgnpe} and \texttt{ntn060cz}; a run that
kept training is \texttt{o053grx1} (\cref{tab:night-runs} links each).
\src{notes/experiments.019-simb-multimodal.scripts.gh_expr_v22_fast.md}

\pfstep{Four layers at width 180 did not train at the reference rate} Both split seeds
launched and collapsed, at epochs 215 and 119, and were stopped near epoch 310. No wider
trunk has yet been run with a warmup or a lower rate, so this is a statement about one
setting.

\pfstep{The Hadamard operator is behind the softmax operator at this budget} On the warmup
arm, with the same split seeds, the Hadamard operator of v21's S\_hadam reads
\nightHadamWindows{} at the window, against the softmax operator \nightHadamVsWarmup. Its
heads launch later and its curves are still the steepest at epoch 1{,}199, so the read is
of this budget; in the two-hour grid of \cref{sec:status} it led at epoch 120, which shows
how little an early read predicts. v21 carries the same contrast at batch 32 on twelve
split seeds.

\pfstep{Every curve dips and is still climbing at 1{,}200 epochs} On each surviving run the
validation Pearson rises early (to 0.10 to 0.12 near epoch 200 on split seed 2), falls
through epochs 400 to 800 while the train Pearson climbs past 0.4, and rises again; between
epochs 1{,}000 and 1{,}199 the 20-epoch mean still gains about 0.02 (the ladder columns of
\cref{tab:night-runs}). The registered window therefore reads a budget and not a plateau,
as the audit of \cref{sec:review} found for the longer runs.

\pfstep{Two regularizers at 800 epochs} On the warmup arm, weight decay raised from
$10^{-8}$ to 0.3 and dropout raised from 0.1 to 0.3 were each run for 800 epochs and read
against the warmup arm at matched epochs. At epoch 400, in the dip, weight decay is
\nightDecayVsWarmupEarly, and dropout is \nightDropVsWarmupEarly. At epoch 799 weight decay
is \nightDecayVsWarmupLate, and dropout is \nightDropVsWarmupLate. Runs collapsed:
\nightDecayCollapsed{} of 3 under weight decay and \nightDropCollapsed{} of 3 under dropout.
The 800-epoch runs stop before the registered window, so these are matched-epoch reads and
not window scores.

\pfstep{Two further speed levers, timed for 40 epochs each} With three batch-128 runs on a
card the new code runs a plain epoch in 8.8 to 9.5 s and an epoch that carries the eval-mode
train pass in 21.5 to 22.5 s. Narrowing the operator's feed-forward block from four times
the width to one takes the plain epoch to 8.0 to 8.5 s, about a tenth, and frees 3.4 GB of
the card; whether the narrower block scores the same is not measured. A single batch-256
run alone on a card takes 3.0 s per plain epoch and 6.0 s with the eval pass, in 19.6 GB,
so two fit on a card and a 1{,}200-epoch run takes about an hour. One batch-256 run at the
unscaled rate was then trained for 1{,}000 epochs on split seed 0: at epoch 799 it is
\nightBigBatchVsLrOne{} against the batch-128 unscaled arm and \nightBigBatchVsRef{} against
the reference, one split seed each.
The timing runs are in W\&B project \texttt{torchcell\_019\_profile} (GilaHyper job 3332).
\src{notes/experiments.019-simb-multimodal.scripts.gh_profile_cgt_expr.md}


\pfstep{What follows for the next rounds} New rounds should run on the new code with the
splits in memory, zero loader workers on Delta, and one arm per card. Batch 128 at the
unscaled rate is the candidate default if its difference from the reference above is
acceptable to the author: it halves the time per epoch and has not collapsed in three runs.
Any arm that raises the learning rate needs a warmup. Run time is to be projected from the
logged epoch seconds over at least 20 epochs, never from the progress bar. The decisions
that are the author's: whether the other 26 packs of v21 are replaced in place, resubmitted,
or left to stop near epoch 740 to 820 (the 15:33 read: 230 s per epoch, not the 177 s of the first eleven hours); and whether the registered window should move later, given
that every curve is still rising at 1{,}200.
